sections.title: Key topic 1: The development of the civil rights movement, 1954–60

topics.title: 1 The position of Black Americans in the early 1950s

points.point_text: **Racial segregation, social discrimination, and voting rights in Southern states.**: Jim Crow Laws: Southern states legally enforced racial segregation in schools, transit, and public accommodations.; Voter Disenfranchisement: Authorities used arbitrary literacy tests, poll taxes, and violent intimidation to prevent Black citizens from registering to vote.; Separate but Equal: The 1896 Plessy v. Ferguson Supreme Court ruling established this legal doctrine, though Black facilities were consistently inferior.

points.point_text: **The efforts and campaigns of civil rights groups, specifically the NAACP and CORE.**: NAACP: The National Association for the Advancement of Colored People focused on legal challenges to segregation, led by Thurgood Marshall.; CORE: The Congress of Racial Equality pioneered non-violent direct action, organizing early sit-ins and boycotts.

topics.title: 2 Progress in education and legal challenges

points.point_text: **The causes, core features, and historical impact of the Brown v. Topeka ruling (1954).**: Supreme Court Ruling: Chief Justice Earl Warren led a unanimous (9-0) decision declaring that segregated public schools violated the 14th Amendment's Equal Protection Clause.; Doctrine Overturned: The court declared that separate educational facilities are 'inherently unequal,' dismantling the constitutional basis for Jim Crow.; Southern Resistance: Southern politicians signed the 'Southern Manifesto' and formed White Citizens' Councils to delay and block school integration.

points.point_text: **The causes, key developments, and importance of the desegregation crisis at Little Rock Central High School (1957).**: Faubus' Defiance: Arkansas Governor Orval Faubus deployed the state's National Guard to block nine Black students from enrolling at Central High School in Little Rock.; Federal Intervention: President Eisenhower federalized the Arkansas National Guard and sent the 101st Airborne Division to escort the students to classes.; Cold War Context: Eisenhower intervened partly to defend the nation's international reputation, as Soviet propaganda weaponized images of racial violence.

sections.title: Key topic 2: Protest, progress and radicalism, 1960–75

points.point_text: **The impact of the Greensboro sit-ins and the growth of the student movement.**: Greensboro Sit-in (1960): Four Black college students sat at a segregated Woolworth's lunch counter, refusing to leave after being denied service.; Rapid Spread: This action sparked a wave of sit-ins across the South, involving over 70,000 students and desegregating hundreds of public counters.; SNCC Founded: The movement led directly to the creation of the Student Nonviolent Coordinating Committee (SNCC) to coordinate student protests.
points.teacher_note: ⚠️ UNEXAMINED TOPIC: This specification point has never appeared on an official Edexcel paper since 2018. It is prime territory for an upcoming series.

points.point_text: **The causes, key events, and impact of the Freedom Rides, including white supremacist violence and the Anniston bus bombing (1961).**: CORE Campaign: Activists rode interstate buses into the deep South to test federal rulings outlawing transit segregation.; Anniston Bombing: An angry white mob firebombed a Freedom Riders' bus in Anniston, Alabama, and beat the escaping passengers.; Federal Action: The extreme violence forced Attorney General Robert Kennedy to issue a strict ban on transit segregation.
points.teacher_note: ⚠️ UNEXAMINED TOPIC: This specification point has never appeared on an official Edexcel paper since 2018. It is prime territory for an upcoming series.

points.point_text: **The desegregation of the University of Mississippi and the James Meredith case (1962).**: Ole Miss Desegregation: James Meredith won a federal court order to enroll at the all-white University of Mississippi.; Federal Force: Governor Ross Barnett physically blocked him, sparking riots that forced President Kennedy to send 30,000 federal troops to secure Meredith's safety.

topics.title: 2 Birmingham, Washington and the Civil Rights Act 1964
